builder_plan.scenario: A workflow needs specialist review, but extra agents may add more cost than useful work.
builder_plan.change: Test the proposed division of work against a single-agent implementation.
builder_plan.baseline: One agent with the same tools and an equal total token and time budget.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.

Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.

builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: ATC: Agent Trajectory Control for Role-Contract Enforcement in Black-Box Multi-Agent Systems
summary: ATC replaces implicit role separation via prompting or fixed workflow graphs with an explicit per-role contract and a gate that scores each proposed message for out-of-role deviation, leakage into other roles' functions, impermissible speech acts, and contract breaches, then constrains regeneration and re-checks before admission. It costs an additional scoring-and-possible-regeneration step per message, adding latency and API or GPU inference calls on every turn, plus the engineering burden of authoring and maintaining role contracts. It can fail through misclassification of legitimate cross-role messages (blocking useful behavior or looping regenerations), poorly specified contracts, and dependence on a scorer whose own reliability bounds the enforcement quality.
rationale: The method is black-box and message-level, so it is compatible with third-party APIs and small teams running multi-agent pipelines, but the abstract provides no quantitative results or cost measurements, so its benefit-to-latency trade-off must be validated on the reader's own workload before production adoption.

claims.statement: ATC replaces implicit role separation via prompting or fixed workflow graphs with an explicit per-role contract and a gate that scores each proposed message for out-of-role deviation, leakage into other roles' functions, impermissible speech acts, and contract breaches, then constrains regeneration and re-checks before admission. It costs an additional scoring-and-possible-regeneration step per message, adding latency and API or GPU inference calls on every turn, plus the engineering burden of authoring and maintaining role contracts. It can fail through misclassification of legitimate cross-role messages (blocking useful behavior or looping regenerations), poorly specified contracts, and dependence on a scorer whose own reliability bounds the enforcement quality.

The abstract claims ATC improves task performance and role consistency while lowering role-drift energy relative to prompting, memory, workflow-control, and activation-editing baselines, with the largest gains under role-confusion stress tests and in larger, more diverse teams; no quantitative factor is given in the abstract.
